title: Fame forgets
hookLine: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)
last: RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE, WITHOUT SWERVING.

cards: Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them, without looking anything up. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world.
Three generations on, some of their names have slipped even from their own family.
Marcus Aurelius, whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself, and used it to loosen the grip of wanting to be remembered. Today: fame forgets.

teach.h: EVERYONE WHO REMEMBERS WILL DIE TOO.
teach.b: In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death.

teach.h: EVEN IF THEY DIDN'T, WHAT IS IT TO YOU?
teach.b: They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die.
Then he pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you?
Praise can't reach the dead. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? Information, at best.
It doesn't make the act better or worse. So what's left is the act itself. Do good to be remembered, and you're building on something that will dissolve.

teach.h: THE ACT IS COMPLETE WHEN DONE.
teach.b: Do it because it's good, and it's complete the moment it's done. This can sound bleak. But look at the questions it answers: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me?

In the end, nobody will remember. So the good thing can be done without an audience, the way a great-grandmother might once have fed a neighbor's child and never written it down. Her name may be gone.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

o: memory fades, so a good act needn't wait to be remembered
you should hide every good deed you do from your family
only well-known people's good deeds last through history

p: passed on until it goes out

s: Marcus says the people who remember you will keep your memory alive
he says each of them will soon die too, until the whole memory goes out.
Marcus asks what lasting memory would be to you even if it lasted
you'd be gone; praise can't reach the dead.
Marcus says praise to the living makes an act better
he asks what praise is, except for some practical use.

games.q: you fixed a mistake that would have cost your team a week. nobody noticed. what fits Meditations 4.19?
o: make sure everyone hears about it.
let it stand, complete, without credit.
games.why: Marcus says memory and praise both fade; the good act is already whole, credited or not.

practice: Think of someone in your family line whose name you don't know, two or three generations back, and picture them at the end of an ordinary day, having done some small good nobody wrote down. Let them be uncredited, and complete.
Then think of one good you could do for no credit, something nobody will know was you.

wordCard.voice: Fame forgets. Marcus notes that everyone who remembers you will die too; so do good for its own sake, complete without credit. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'after-fame', fame after death: the craving Marcus answers in 4.19. The same word ends book two: after-fame is oblivion.

carryVoice: Your line: no credit. Done well, and done, is enough, credited or not. See you tomorrow.
